LESSON 69 OF 106·Web and Application Security Basics

Browser Defences: CSP, HSTS, SameSite and CSRF Tokens

What each browser-side control actually stops, why a policy limits damage rather than the bug, and how a CSRF token proves intent rather than guarding a secret.

Foundation2 min
Why this matters

These are the browser-side defences that limit what happens when something else goes wrong. None of them prevents a vulnerability; each of them reduces how much an attacker gets from one.

INTERACTIVE FLOW MODEL

  1. Vector: An attacker or faulty client alters parameters, headers, timing, or sequence order.
  2. Weakness: Check the response headers directly, because configuration that works locally may not reach production.
  3. Impact: The component trusts unverified data, crossing a confidentiality or integrity boundary.
01 Untrusted Input
Enforced control
02 Server Policy Gate
Verified
03 Verified Operation
  1. Verification: Send a content security policy in report-only mode, fix what it flags, then enforce without unsafe-inline.
  2. Enforcement: Checks run deterministically on the server side for every sensitive action.
  3. Resilience: Invalid requests fail closed and emit structured security telemetry.

What you'll learn

By the end of this lesson you can:

  • check the response headers directly, because configuration that works locally may not reach production
  • check whether the session cookie has Secure, HttpOnly and an appropriate SameSite value
  • check whether a content security policy is enforced or only reported
  • check whether any state-changing action relies solely on a cookie with no token

How it works

  • A content security policy tells the browser which sources of script, style and frames are allowed, so injected script may simply not run.
  • HTTP strict transport security tells the browser to refuse plaintext, which removes a network-level downgrade.
  • SameSite on cookies decides whether they are attached to cross-site requests, which is the mechanism behind most cross-site request forgery.
  • A cross-site request forgery token is a value the attacker cannot read, so a forged request cannot include it.
  • These controls work together: one blocks the script, one blocks the request, and the other forces the browser to a safe protocol.

The background

  • These headers were added to browsers one at a time, and adoption lagged for years because they broke real applications.
  • Report-only modes were introduced so sites could measure impact before enforcing, which is the only realistic adoption path.
  • Modern frameworks enable them by default, which has moved them from an expert concern to a baseline expectation.
  • Third-party script requirements are the main reason policies stay permissive, which is the same trust problem as before.

Real-world examples

  • A site with no content security policy turns one stored scripting flaw into a complete account takeover.
  • A session cookie with no SameSite attribute is sent on cross-site requests, which is exactly what makes forgery work.
  • HSTS missing from a site allows a network attacker to downgrade the first request, which is often the only one that matters.

What to look for

  • Check the response headers directly, because configuration that works locally may not reach production.
  • Check whether the session cookie has Secure, HttpOnly and an appropriate SameSite value.
  • Check whether a content security policy is enforced or only reported.
  • Check whether any state-changing action relies solely on a cookie with no token.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Send a content security policy in report-only mode, fix what it flags, then enforce without unsafe-inline.
  • Set Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite on every session cookie, and use the strictest SameSite your flows allow.
  • Enable HTTP strict transport security, including preloading once you are confident it will not break anything.
  • Require a token on every state-changing request, and treat the token check as the authorisation check too.
  • Test with the headers enabled in a real browser, since some failures only appear with a real session.
